edges.why: Knowing what a kilometer, meter, and centimeter actually look like lets the learner say which is longer.
The statement says one unit is 1000 times or 100 times as long as another, a multiplicative comparison.
Knowing real lengths of an inch, foot, and yard lets the learner say which of two units is longer.
The statement says a foot is 12 times as long as an inch, a multiplicative comparison of lengths.
The learner must already know grams and kilograms as units of mass to say which is heavier.
The statement says a kilogram is 1000 times as heavy as a gram, a multiplicative comparison.
The learner must know ounces and pounds as units of weight, from weighing objects, to compare them.
The statement says a pound is 16 times as heavy as an ounce, a multiplicative comparison.
The learner must know liters and milliliters as units of liquid volume to say which holds more.
The statement says a liter is 1000 times as much liquid as a milliliter, a multiplicative comparison.
Hours and minutes must already be familiar clock units before their relative sizes can be stated as a fact.
The statement says an hour is 60 times as long as a minute, a multiplicative comparison of durations.
The assess asks whether the number of smaller units is more or less than the number of larger units.
The statement says the smaller-unit number is k times the larger-unit number, a multiplicative comparison.
The reason given is that each larger unit is replaced by k smaller ones, so n larger units make n groups of k.
Each row of the table is (n, n x k), which is the multiplicative relation between the two units.
The statement defines a two-column table, so the learner must read and fill entries by row and column.
Completing the yards-to-feet rows requires the products 3 x 1 through 3 x 5.
The statement that n larger units equal n x k smaller units is the multiplicative relation of units.
Step 2 multiplies the count of larger units by k, such as 7 x 1000, a whole number times a one-digit number.
Step 1 converts the a larger units to a x k smaller units, exactly the whole-number conversion.
Step 2 adds the b leftover smaller units to the converted amount, such as 120 + 15.
Converting a decimal amount to the smaller unit rests on the smaller-unit count being k times the larger.
Step 2 multiplies the decimal by 10, 100, or 1000, which moves the decimal point right.
The statement that a/b larger units equal (a/b) x k smaller units is the multiplicative relation of units.
Step 2 multiplies the fraction a/b by the whole number k, which is fraction times whole number.
Finding 3/4 of 60 gives 180/4, which must be divided out to get 45 minutes.
Dividing n by k is justified because n smaller units are a multiple of k and each k smaller units make one larger.
The number of larger units is the number of groups of k smaller units in n, the grouping meaning of a quotient.
Step 2 divides the number of smaller units by k, which is often two-digit such as 72 divided by 12.
The q larger units come from converting the part of n that is an exact multiple of k, as in the whole-number case.
Step 2 divides n by k to get a whole-number quotient and remainder, such as 200 divided by 60.
Dividing by the power of ten is justified because the smaller-unit count is that power of ten times the larger-unit count.
Step 2 divides the measurement by 10, 100, or 1000, which moves the decimal point left.
The result is written as a decimal in tenths, hundredths, or thousandths of the larger unit.
Each smaller unit is one k-th of the larger unit because the smaller-unit count is k times the larger.
Step 2 writes the number of smaller units over k as n/k, using that a divided by b equals a/b.
Nine inches is 9 parts of size 1/12 of a foot, the non-unit fraction as a count of unit parts.
The statement allows the result to be a mixed number, a whole number plus a fraction.
The measurement is shown as the point that many units from 0, a whole number as a length on a number line.
Reading a labeled scale as units counted from the 0 mark is the same idea as reading a ruler.
Locating 700 mL on a scale with a mark every 100 mL means counting seven marks by hundreds from 0.
The statement is a one- or two-step word problem with multi-digit whole numbers in a measurement context.
Cutting 260 cm into 4 equal pieces requires dividing 260 by 4.
Cutting 15 cm off a 65 cm piece requires subtracting 65 - 15.
The statement allows an interval that crosses the hour, as 2:50 plus 25 minutes does.
Finding an end time by adding an interval in minutes to a start time is one case of the statement.
Finding a start time by subtracting an interval in minutes from an end time is one case of the statement.
Crossing the hour means regrouping 60 minutes as 1 hour, which uses the hour-minute relation.
The statement includes two-step problems, such as adding a bus ride and then a walk.
Combining fractional distances or amounts of one unit is adding fractions of the same whole in a story.
Finding how much more or less between fractional measures is subtracting fractions of the same whole in a story.
The statement allows mixed-number measurements, which are added with like denominators.
The statement allows mixed-number measurements, which are subtracted with like denominators.
Amounts are written with a dollar sign and decimal point, the money notation.
A cents amount in dollars such as 2.75 is a decimal in hundredths.
Money word problems about combining amounts extend the earlier coin-and-dollar addition stories.
Money word problems about change and differences extend the earlier coin-and-dollar subtraction stories.
Finding the cost of a notebook and a pen together is a sum of two amounts such as 275 cents and 140 cents.
The statement requires first expressing the larger-unit measurement in the smaller unit, as 3 m in centimeters.
After the conversion the problem is a one- or two-step whole-number problem in a single unit.
The statement allows converting to a smaller unit with a whole-number result.
The statement allows converting to a larger unit with a whole-number result.
The statement allows converting to a smaller unit with a decimal result.
The statement allows converting to a larger unit with a decimal result, as 3750 m to 3.75 km.
The statement allows converting to a smaller unit with a fraction result.
The statement allows converting to a larger unit with a fraction result.
The statement is a multi-step real-world problem with multi-digit numbers in which conversion is one step.
Finding the total of 750 m run on each of 5 days is a multiplication by a one-digit number.
The statement uses A = l x w for a rectangle, with the area and one side known.
The unknown side is the unknown factor, so the quotient is read as a missing factor.
Step 1 writes A = l x w with a symbol standing for the unknown side.
Step 2 divides the area by the known side, such as 96 divided by 12.
The statement includes finding an area of a rectangle in a real-world setting.
The statement includes finding an unknown side length from the area, as in 180 square feet and 15 feet.
The formula generalizes the procedure of adding the four side lengths found from a length and width.
The formula is written with letters l and w in an expression, and the assess chooses among expressions.
Two sides of each length is 2 equal groups, so 2 x l and 2 x w record the equal sides.
The reason given about opposite sides being equal depends on knowing what a rectangle is.
The statement that l + w is half the perimeter comes from P = 2 x l + 2 x w.
Step 1 divides the perimeter by 2 to find the sum of a length and a width.
Step 2 subtracts the known side from that half-perimeter, such as 15 - 9.
The statement uses P = 2 x l + 2 x w to model the real-world situation.
The statement includes finding an unknown side from the perimeter, as in the fence problem.
The statement includes finding a perimeter in a real-world setting from a length and width.
Making a line plot with halves and fourths is the same representation, extended here to eighths.
Step 2 partitions each whole unit and labels the marks, locating non-unit fractions on the number line.
Choosing the finest part means placing halves and fourths at the same points as equivalent eighths.
The pencil lengths such as 5 1/2 and 6 1/4 are mixed numbers to be placed between whole-number marks.
The learner must read each X on a fraction scale as a fractional measurement from the number line.
Adding fractional measurements marked on one fraction scale is adding fractions with a common denominator.
Subtracting fractional measurements marked on one fraction scale is subtracting fractions with a common denominator.
How much longer the longest insect is than the shortest is a subtraction as comparison.
The statement starts from reading fractional data off a line plot and adding or subtracting it.
Totaling measurements such as 1/4 and 1/2 on one plot uses fraction addition with unlike denominators.
Differences of plotted measurements such as 3/4 and 1/2 use subtraction with unlike denominators.
The statement lists multiplication of fractions among the operations combined with the plot data.
Equal redistribution of a total shares a fraction among a whole number of containers, a fraction divided by a whole number.
The total of 4 liters shared among 6 beakers is 4 divided by 6, which equals the fraction 4/6.
The statement measures an angle between its two rays at a common vertex.
The measure is a fraction of a circle, such as 1/8 or 3/8, that lies between the rays.
A one-degree angle is defined as the angle that turns through a fraction of a circle.
The fraction 1/360 is a unit fraction, one of 360 equal parts, so 360 of them fill the circle.
The statement counts one-degree angles that fill an angle with no gaps or overlaps to name its measure.
Step 1 identifies the fraction of the circle the angle turns through.
The factor 360 comes from a full circle being made of 360 one-degree angles.
Step 3 labels the product in degrees, the count of one-degree angles.
Step 2 multiplies the fraction a/b by 360, a fraction times a whole number.
Finding 3/8 of 360 gives 1080/8, which is divided to get 135 degrees.
The protractor reading is a count of one-degree angles from the 0 mark to the other ray.
Step 1 places the center on the vertex, so the learner must identify the vertex and rays.
Step 3 reads a degree number from a scale with marks between the labeled numbers.
Placing the center and 0 mark on the ray and reading the same scale are the measuring skills used in reverse.
The angle drawn has the given measure in degrees, a count of one-degree angles.
Step 1 draws a ray with one endpoint, which is the side of the angle.
The whole angle is filled by the one-degree angles of its parts, so the measures add.
The statement splits an angle by a ray from its vertex into two angles sharing that vertex.
Finding the whole angle needs the sum 30 + 45.
The whole equals the known part plus the unknown part, which is why subtracting finds the unknown part.
Finding the other part is finding the unknown addend that completes the whole.
Step 2 subtracts the known part from the whole, such as 90 - 35.
The equation states that the parts add to the whole angle, which is additivity of angle measure.
The statement uses a symbol for the unknown measure.
Writing an addition or subtraction equation with a symbol for the unknown from a situation is the same representing skill, here from a diagram.
The statement includes problems in which one part of the angle is unknown, found by subtracting.
The statement includes problems in which the whole angle is unknown, found by adding parts.
The unit cube is a cube, which has six equal square faces and equal edges.
The statement defines the cube by edges each 1 unit long, a length measured in units.
Rejecting a 1 cm square as a volume unit requires telling a flat shape from a solid.
Volume is measured in units that are unit cubes, each with a volume of one cubic unit.
Counting cubes gives the volume only because a solid packed with n unit cubes has volume n cubic units.
Step 2 counts every cube in the solid, including cubes hidden behind or under others.
Step 3 reports the count in cubic units of the cube used.
Each layer of the prism is an array of a by b cubes, a product shown as a rectangle.
The number of cubes in the prism is its volume in cubic units.
Reading a x b x c as c layers of a x b cubes groups the three factors in the associative way.
The explanation uses the prism of l x w x h unit cubes with its three edge lengths.
Counting all the packed cubes is the definition of volume the explanation starts from.
Each layer is an l by w array whose count l x w equals the base area in square units.
The formula says the number of unit cubes in a prism is the product of its three edge lengths.
The formula gives the volume in cubic units as a count of packed unit cubes.
The formula is written as an expression with the letters l, w, and h.
The procedure multiplies the three edge lengths, as the formula V = l x w x h says.
Step 2 multiplies the three edge lengths, such as 8 x 5 x 3, by one-digit multiplications.
Step 3 labels the product in cubic units, which are unit cubes.
Base area times height is one of the three equal counts the layers explanation shows.
The formula gives the volume as the number of cubes that pack the prism.
The base B is the area of a rectangle in square units, found as length times width.
The formula is written as an expression with the letters B and h.
The procedure multiplies base area by height, as the formula V = B x h says.
Step 1 finds the base area of the rectangular base when it is not given.
Step 2 multiplies the base area by the height, such as 35 x 6.
Step 3 labels the product in cubic units, which are unit cubes.
The statement allows solving by V = l x w x h with the three edge lengths.
The statement allows solving by V = B x h from a base area and a height.
The fish tank problem multiplies 24 x 12 x 16, which has multi-digit factors.
Volume is a count of unit cubes, so the cubes of non-overlapping parts add.
Joining boxes of 24 and 18 cubic feet requires adding 24 + 18.
Adding the volumes of the two prisms is justified by volume being additive over non-overlapping parts.
Step 1 splits the L-shaped face into two rectangles, the same decomposing used for rectilinear area.
Step 2 subtracts given lengths to find an unlabeled edge, such as 10 - 3.
Step 3 finds the volume of each prism by multiplying its three edge lengths.
Step 4 adds the two volumes, such as 96 and 60.
The statement is a real-world problem solved by splitting the solid, finding each volume, and adding.
